description: How criminal and civil law differ in purpose, parties, courts and outcomes.
content_html:
Two Types of Law

Not every legal dispute involves a crime. When a landlord fails to return a tenant’s deposit, when an employer pays someone less than the law requires, or when a business delivers faulty goods, these situations are handled through civil law. By contrast, when someone commits an act that society has decided is harmful enough to deserve state punishment — theft, assault, fraud — this falls under criminal law. Understanding the difference is fundamental to GCSE Citizenship and to everyday life.

Key Fact

In criminal law, the state prosecutes the accused. In civil law, a private individual or organisation (the claimant) brings a case against another (the defendant). Criminal cases must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; civil cases are decided on the balance of probabilities. Criminal outcomes include imprisonment or fines; civil outcomes typically involve compensation or an injunction.

Criminal Law in Detail

Criminal law defines acts that are offences against society as a whole, not just against the immediate victim. When a burglar breaks into a house, the case is brought by the state (technically the Crown) against the accused — not by the householder personally. The prosecution presents evidence to a court to show that the accused committed the offence. The accused person is the defendant.

The standard of proof is high: guilt must be established beyond reasonable doubt. This protects defendants from wrongful conviction. If found guilty, the court can impose a range of sentences, including a fine, community order, suspended sentence or custodial sentence (imprisonment). The aims of criminal sentencing are retribution, deterrence, public protection, rehabilitation and reparation. Different sentences may prioritise different aims depending on the offence and the offender’s circumstances.

Criminal cases are heard in different courts depending on severity. Magistrates’ courts deal with summary offences and less serious either-way offences. Magistrates are unpaid volunteers advised on law by a legal clerk; they can impose fines and sentences of up to 12 months (or up to 6 months per offence for multiple counts). The vast majority of criminal cases — around 95% — are resolved in magistrates’ courts.

More serious offences (indictable offences) are heard in the Crown Court. Here, a judge presides over the trial and a jury of twelve members of the public decides the verdict. The Crown Court can impose unlimited sentences for the most serious offences. Appeals from the Crown Court go to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) and, in exceptional cases, to the Supreme Court.

Civil Law in Detail

Civil law deals with disputes between private parties. The person who brings the case is the claimant (formerly called the plaintiff). The person or organisation being sued is the defendant. The claimant must show, on the balance of probabilities, that the defendant is legally responsible for the harm caused. If the court finds in the claimant’s favour, it may award damages (financial compensation) or grant an injunction (a court order requiring the defendant to stop a certain action).

Civil disputes cover a wide range of everyday situations: breach of contract (a company does not deliver goods as agreed), negligence (a driver injures a pedestrian through careless driving), defamation (someone publishes false statements that damage another’s reputation), employment disputes (unfair dismissal, discrimination at work), and family law matters (divorce, child custody). The purpose of civil law is not punishment but remedy — putting the injured party back, as far as possible, in the position they were in before the harm occurred.

A very common error in GCSE Citizenship exams is to assume that any harmful or wrongful act is a crime. This is not the case. Whether an act is treated as criminal or civil depends on Parliament’s decision about whether the harm is serious enough to merit state prosecution and punishment. A building company that cuts corners and builds a structurally unsafe wall may face a civil claim for negligence from the property owner — but the same act might also result in a criminal prosecution under Health and Safety law. The same act can sometimes trigger both criminal proceedings and a civil claim, though these are separate processes. The terms used in each system are also different: in criminal law you have a “prosecution”, a “defendant” and a “conviction”; in civil law you have a “claim”, a “claimant” and a “judgment”.

Civil Courts

Most civil disputes in England and Wales are heard in the County Court. More complex or high-value claims go to the High Court. For claims under £10,000, a simplified “small claims track” allows individuals to bring cases without needing a solicitor, though legal advice can still help. Employment disputes are heard in employment tribunals, which are specialist bodies designed to be more accessible than courts for resolving workplace disputes.

Tribunals and alternative dispute resolution (ADR) methods such as mediation and arbitration provide quicker, cheaper routes to resolving civil disputes without going to court. ADR encourages parties to reach an agreed settlement. Many contracts now include arbitration clauses requiring disputes to be resolved this way rather than through the courts.

Key Fact

Three legal systems operate within the UK. England and Wales share one system based on common law and Parliamentary legislation. Scotland has its own distinct legal system (Scots law), with different terminology and courts including the Sheriff Court and the Court of Session. Northern Ireland has a separate legal system based on common law. The UK Supreme Court is the final court of appeal for civil cases from all three systems and for criminal cases from England, Wales and Northern Ireland (not Scotland, where the High Court of Justiciary is the final criminal appeal court).
exam_tip_html: The criminal/civil distinction is tested frequently in short-answer and extended-response questions. The most common errors are: (1) using the wrong terminology — calling the person who brings a civil case the “prosecutor” when the correct term is “claimant”; (2) stating that both criminal and civil cases use “beyond reasonable doubt” — civil cases use the lower “balance of probabilities” standard; (3) failing to link the standard of proof to its justification — examiners reward answers that explain why criminal cases use a higher standard (the consequences of a wrongful conviction include imprisonment). For 8-mark Analyse questions, you will usually be asked to analyse advantages and disadvantages of one system, or to compare the two. Always name a specific court (magistrates’ court, Crown Court, County Court, employment tribunal) or a specific outcome (damages, injunction, imprisonment) to demonstrate precise knowledge and reach the higher bands.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Criminal law involves the state prosecuting a defendant for an offence against society; the standard of proof is beyond reasonable doubt; outcomes include fines, community orders or imprisonment.
  • Civil law involves a claimant bringing a case against a defendant for a private dispute; the standard of proof is the balance of probabilities; outcomes typically include compensation (damages) or an injunction.
  • The UK has three separate legal systems (England and Wales; Scotland; Northern Ireland), and a range of courts from magistrates’ courts and the Crown Court (criminal) to the County Court, High Court and employment tribunals (civil), with the UK Supreme Court as the final civil appeal court across all three systems.

practice_questions.text:
In a civil law case, what is the name given to the person who brings the case?
A) Prosecutor
B) Defendant
C) Claimant
D) Barrister
Identify two differences between criminal law and civil law.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of any two genuinely distinct differences from the following or equivalent:
• In criminal law the state brings the prosecution; in civil law a private individual or organisation (the claimant) brings the case.
• Criminal cases must be proved beyond reasonable doubt; civil cases are decided on the balance of probabilities.
• Criminal outcomes include imprisonment or fines; civil outcomes typically involve compensation (damages) or injunctions.
• Criminal cases are heard in magistrates' courts or the Crown Court; civil cases are heard in the County Court or High Court.
• The purpose of criminal law is to punish and deter; the purpose of civil law is to provide a remedy for the person harmed.

Near-duplicate answers (e.g. two ways of stating the same standard-of-proof point) score once only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of how criminal cases are heard in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per feature described. Credit two developed points from the following or equivalent:
• Magistrates' courts deal with less serious (summary) offences; magistrates are unpaid volunteers who can impose fines and short custodial sentences (1 for the point; 2 for development adding e.g. that around 95% of cases are resolved here).
• The Crown Court hears more serious (indictable) offences and uses a jury of twelve members of the public to decide the verdict, with a judge presiding (1 for the point; 2 for development).
• The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt — this is a higher standard than civil law to protect against wrongful conviction (1 for the point; 2 for development).
• Possible sentences include fines, community service, suspended sentences and custodial sentences depending on the severity of the offence (1 for the point; 2 for development naming and explaining two sentence types).

Do not credit evaluation — description only.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional advice leaflet produced by a local citizens’ advice charity states: 'Last year, over 60% of the queries we received about legal problems involved civil disputes — mainly employment issues, landlord/tenant disagreements, and consumer contract problems. Many people told us they had not sought formal legal advice because they believed their problem was a criminal matter for the police, or because they thought going to court would be unaffordable. In fact, most of these cases could have been resolved through the small claims track or an employment tribunal at little or no cost.'

What does the source suggest about public understanding of civil law? Use the source and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
1 mark for identifying the source's key finding (many people misidentify civil disputes as criminal matters or believe civil law is unaffordable).
1 mark for interpreting its significance (a lack of public legal literacy may mean people do not access the civil justice remedies they are entitled to).
1 mark for using own knowledge (e.g. the small claims track handles claims under £10,000 with no requirement for a solicitor; employment tribunals are designed to be accessible; the distinction between criminal and civil law is poorly understood by the general public).
1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and knowledge (e.g. the source suggests that the civil justice system could be made more effective by improving public understanding of what civil law covers and what routes to redress are available at low cost).

practice_questions.text: Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of the civil law system in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Sustained two-sided analysis with named examples on each side. Weighs evidence and reaches a substantiated judgement. Names specific courts, procedures or outcomes (County Court, small claims track, employment tribunal, damages, injunction).

Secure (5–6 marks): Both advantages and disadvantages identified and developed. At least one named real-world example. Some weighing.

Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points on one or both sides but development is limited or one-sided.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic relevant points; largely descriptive; little real-world reference.

Advantages to credit: civil law provides a remedy for everyday harms (contract breach, negligence, discrimination) that do not rise to the level of crime; the balance of probabilities standard is more accessible than criminal proof; small claims track and employment tribunals reduce cost and complexity; alternative dispute resolution (mediation, arbitration) offers quicker resolution; civil remedies (damages, injunctions) directly compensate or protect the injured party.

Disadvantages to credit: even with small claims track, legal representation costs can be prohibitive for lower-income claimants; enforcement of civil judgments is not guaranteed — a claimant who wins a damages award still has to pursue the defendant to collect; complex civil cases in the High Court are very expensive and slow; the balance of probabilities standard means a claimant can win a civil case even when there is significant uncertainty about what happened.

practice_questions.text:
"The criminal justice system is more important than the civil justice system because it deals with harm to society as a whole, whereas civil law only protects individual interests."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should consider arguments that support this view, arguments that challenge it, and reach a substantiated conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Full two-sided argument with named examples on each side. Engages with the claim about 'harm to society vs individual interests' and questions or refines it. Reaches a substantiated conclusion that goes beyond 'both are important'.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides developed with at least one named real-world example. Concludes with a partially substantiated judgement.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant arguments on both sides but limited development OR one-sided.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points; little real-world example; largely descriptive.

Arguments supporting the statement: criminal law addresses acts (violence, theft, fraud) that threaten public safety and social order; criminal sanctions (imprisonment) have a deterrence effect that protects society; crime victims include not just the immediate victim but the wider community who feel less safe; the state's role in prosecuting crime reflects that these harms go beyond individual disputes.

Arguments challenging the statement: civil law also protects society-wide interests — employment law, consumer protection and environmental law benefit vast numbers of people, not just individuals; civil remedies for discrimination (e.g. under the Equality Act 2010) have changed workplace culture across entire industries; civil law regulates business conduct and economic life, which affects everyone; without civil law, harmful conduct that falls short of criminality would go unchecked; access to civil justice is a human right (Article 6 ECHR applies to both criminal and civil proceedings); tribunals such as employment tribunals have improved working conditions for millions.

Conclusion to credit: a judgement that goes beyond 'both are equally important' to identify which system has a stronger claim to primacy and why, with reference to named legislation or institutions. Strong answers may challenge the premise by arguing the boundary between the two systems is not fixed — Parliament can make certain civil wrongs criminal (e.g. health and safety breaches) and vice versa.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the standard of proof in a civil case?
Which court hears the majority of criminal cases in England and Wales?
In a civil case, the person who brings the case is called the _____, not the prosecutor.
The most common civil remedy awarded by a court is _____, which is financial compensation paid to the winning party.
Match each term to its correct legal context:
right: The state bringing a case in criminal law
The person bringing a case in civil law
The standard of proof required in criminal cases

flashcard_questions.q: Who brings a criminal case to court?
flashcard_questions.a: The state (the Crown) brings the prosecution against the defendant.

flashcard_questions.q: Who brings a civil case to court?
flashcard_questions.a: A private individual or organisation — the claimant — brings the case.

flashcard_questions.q: What standard of proof applies in criminal cases?
What standard of proof applies in civil cases?
flashcard_questions.a: Balance of probabilities — more likely than not that the claim is true.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the typical outcome of a successful civil case?
flashcard_questions.a: Damages (compensation) or an injunction ordering the defendant to stop a specific action.

flashcard_questions.q: Which court hears the most serious criminal cases in England and Wales?
flashcard_questions.a: The Crown Court, with a judge and jury of twelve.
A lower criminal court where unpaid magistrates hear less serious offences without a jury.
The person or organisation who brings a civil law case claiming their rights have been harmed.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one type of civil dispute handled by an employment tribunal.
flashcard_questions.a: Unfair dismissal claims or workplace discrimination disputes.

flashcard_questions.q: How many legal systems does the UK have?
flashcard_questions.a: Three: England and Wales; Scotland; Northern Ireland.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the small claims track?
flashcard_questions.a: A simplified civil court process for claims under £10,000, designed for use without a solicitor.

flashcard_questions.q: What court is the final court of civil appeal across the whole UK?

glossary_terms.definition: The area of law that governs disputes between private individuals or organisations, where the aim is usually to provide a remedy such as compensation rather than to punish.
The area of law where the state prosecutes individuals who have broken laws that society considers serious enough to warrant punishment.
In a criminal case, the legal process by which the state brings a case against a person accused of a crime.
The person accused of committing a crime in a criminal case.
The person or organisation who brings a case in civil law, claiming that their legal rights have been harmed.
Money paid by the losing party in a civil case to compensate the winning party for loss or harm suffered.
A lower criminal court in England and Wales where magistrates (justices of the peace) hear less serious criminal cases without a jury.
A higher criminal court in England and Wales where serious offences are tried before a judge and jury.
A civil court that handles the majority of civil disputes, including claims for compensation and contract disputes, with jurisdiction over cases up to £100,000.

items.title: In Our Time — The Code of Hammurabi
items.description: The origins of codified law — great context for understanding why modern societies distinguish between criminal and civil wrongs and why written law replaced personal vengeance.

items.title: In Our Time — The Haymarket Affair
items.description: A landmark US criminal trial from 1886 that raised questions about fair procedure and equality before the law — reveals how criminal law can be shaped by political context.

items.title: You Would Be a Terrible Leader — CGP Grey
items.description: The case for systems over individuals — explains why an independent judiciary enforcing the rule of law matters more than the character of any one ruler or judge.

items.title: How to Spot a Misleading Graph — TED-Ed
items.description: Applies critical thinking to data — relevant for evaluating crime statistics and claims made in legal proceedings or media coverage of court cases.

items.title: Twelve Angry Men (1957)
items.description: A jury deliberates the fate of a defendant in a capital murder case — one of the greatest explorations of the presumption of innocence and the standard of 'beyond reasonable doubt' ever filmed.

items.title: The Trial of the Chicago 7 (2020)
items.description: A dramatic criminal trial in which the lines between legitimate protest and criminal conspiracy were contested — useful for exam discussions of where civil disobedience meets criminal law.

items.title: In the Name of the Father (1993)
items.description: The true story of the Guildford Four, wrongly convicted of IRA bombings — a powerful exploration of miscarriages of justice and why the presumption of innocence and rule of law must be protected.

items.title: AQA GCSE Citizenship Studies — Specification
items.description: The official AQA spec — review exactly what is examined on criminal vs civil law, courts, and legal terminology.

items.title: Full Fact — Independent Fact Checking
items.description: The UK's fact-checking organisation — useful for evaluating claims about crime rates, sentencing outcomes and the legal system that appear in the media.
